newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FEATURE - Romania owners, tenants fight over "stolen" homes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Romania owners, tenants fight over "stolen" homes.

text.p: A dispute over the return of nationalised houses has set tenants and former owners at each others' throats as Romania struggles to resolve one of the thorniest issues left by decades of communism.

Some former communist countries have tackled the problem head on, returning appropriated houses and compensating for losses, but in Romania the issue is still a hot political topic ahead of November parliamentary and presidential elections.

Thousands had their homes seized by the shock troops of communism who moved in their families. Many say descendants of the first commissars still run Romania and find it in their interest to make common cause with tenants and stay put.
"I have been living in this apartment for 12 years, taking care of it, so I think I'm entitled to buy it," said Bucharest tenant Mioara Chivulescu.
"I didn't leave my house willingly, my whole family was thrown out in the 50s and we were moved into a cottage," said Zoe Porsenna, former owner of a house in central Bucharest.

Opposition parties support returning property but the leftist ruling Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), in power since December 1989, has issued laws which most political analysts say complicate matters rather than solve the problem.
"Communists annulled our property rights, post-communist democratic rulers have finalised the theft by selling the houses," Porsenna said.
The PDSR pushed through chaotic land reform legislation in 1991 to win votes among the peasantry, dismantling collectives and doling out 10 hectare (25 acre) plots to thousands.
But President Ion Iliescu sees no electoral gain in favouring a few middle class voters with property returns and angering many more tenants.

The impasse threatens the fragile fabric of once-beautiful Bucharest, badly damaged by the late dictator Nicolae Ceausescu's destructive building drive, by removing the incentive for anyone to carry out repair work.

"Tenants and former owners may gain or lose from the house restitution law but the worst affected in this whole artificially created hysteria will be the houses themselves," said Dinu Grigorescu, general secretary of Bucharest city hall.
Thousands of Romanians lost property after the communists came to power in 1947 and tried to dismantle capitalism.

Former bankers, factory owners, retailers, land owners and "members of the bourgeoisie" had assets seized by a 1950 decree to "strengthen and develop the socialist economy and take from exploiters an important means of exploitation."
The 1950 decree said houses belonging to "workers, employees, intellectuals and pensioners will not be nationalised," but an owner's social status was often ignored.
"My father, a state employee for all his life, built a three-flat house for our family, but we were thrown out of it," said 71-year-old Cristina Marinescu.
She pointed to a photograph of her house: "This is all I have left now of my father's lifetime work -- a picture.
"Nationalisation was a hurricane. Whole streets were swept clean to create enclaves for communist leaders to move in."
Some 240,000 houses were taken by the Soviet-installed communists and given to the emerging "nomenklatura" class of state functionaries. Some 154,000 have since been demolished.
Among these houses, many of them built in the booming 1930s, were fabulous villas and palazzos in the most desirable northern districts of Bucharest.
Many are now in the hands of politicians, some 180 of whom were condemned last year by a parliamentary commission for illegally acquiring the attractive dwellings.

A law pushed through both houses of parliament by the leftist government and neo-communist allies last year that attempts to bring Romania up to European Union legal standards allows only a tiny minority to claim back lost homes.
Most dispossessed Romanians, including expatriates, will get compensation worth a maximum 50 million lei ($16,000). That sum will buy a one-room flat in a communist-era block.
Tenants lucky enough to find themselves in an elegant downtown flat can buy it relatively cheaply. Prices range from 100,000 lei ($32) to 300,000 lei ($94) per square metre (square yard).
Grigorescu said that more than 40,000 tenants in Bucharest had asked to buy flats while only some 9,000 former owners had claimed restitution or compensation for their properties.
"It will be a titanic work to clear the status of these houses, each being a unique case which must be considered carefully," said Grigorescu.
Opposition parties say the state should not sell confiscated houses because it does not legally own them.

"The law can solve nothing by putting tenants and owners in conflict," said Victor Surdu, head of the Democratic Agrarian Party. Surdu stunned public opinion when he gave up his right to buy his house and returned it to the former owner.
"To buy a house taken by force and illegally from somebody is like a curse, it's not moral," he said.
